newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Reliance poised for sharp drop in profit.
newsitem.headline: India's Reliance poised for sharp drop in profit.

text.p: India's Reliance Industries Ltd is heading for a steep fall in post-tax profit for the six months ended September 30, a Reuters poll of leading brokerages showed on Tuesday.
Net profit forecasts for Reliance by 14 major securities firms averaged 4.7 billion rupees ($131.6 million), 25.8 percent down from the first six months of the previous year.
Sales were forecast to fall 21.1 percent to an average 31.3 billion rupees during the period.
"The fall entirely reflects the fall in polyester fibre and yarn selling prices during the year," said V.V. Sivakumar, head of research at Peregrine Capital India.
"Polyester yarn prices in the first six months on an average are about 27 percent down compared to the previous half year," said Jal Irani, analyst at Jardine Fleming India Broking.
The price drop for polyester fibre has been even steeper, falling by about 30 percent year-on-year, Irani said. Reliance is India's largest producer of polyester and its raw materials.
An analyst at a European securities firm in Bombay said that polyester as a percentage of Reliance's total sales would fall to 50 percent this year from more than 55 percent last year.
"This is entirely because of the price fall. Volumes haven't fallen," said the analyst, who did not want to be identified.
The global fall in polyester price is attributed to sharply reduced imports by China, one of the world's largest importers.
A new 12.9 percent corporate tax imposed in India's federal budget in July will take almost 1.5 billion rupees out of Reliance's profits for the full year ending March 31, 1997, analysts said.
One analyst said he expected Reliance's profits to fall by more than 30 percent, sharper than the Reuters poll's consensus.

High working capital costs despite lower sales turnover this year, and the impact of a 10 percent price hike in Reliance's raw material naphtha in June, would cause profits to plunge by more than 30 percent in the first half, he said.
Volumes should rise in the second half because of expected commissioning of new capacities. But profitability would continue to be depressed by interest and depreciation burdens.
"This year's profits don't matter," said an analyst at a leading Indian brokerage. He said Reliance would see a rise of more than 70 percent in volume growth in 1997/98 (April-March).
The global fall in polyester prices appears to have bottomed out, most analysts said. They said a surge in Reliance's volumes next fiscal year should see a rise in profitability as well.
